hints: Look at what the boiling points tell you first, both are very high so think about what type of giant structures that rules in or out.
Focus on grey tin, it cannot conduct in solid or liquid and is brittle, which giant structure fits a non-conductor with strong bonds?
Now look at white tin, it conducts well even as a solid and can be hammered into shape, so link that behaviour to mobile electrons and layers that can slide.
walkthrough:
**Use boiling point to confirm giant structures**

Both forms have boiling points over 2500 K. That is extremely high.

That tells us strong bonding extends throughout the solid, so both must be giant structures, not simple molecular.

**Identify grey tin from conductivity and brittleness**

Grey tin has no electrical conductivity in solid or liquid, and it is brittle.

A giant covalent lattice like diamond or silicon has all electrons locked in covalent bonds, so no mobile charge carriers to conduct, and the rigid directional bonds make it brittle. This fits grey tin perfectly.

**Identify white tin from conductivity and malleability**

White tin conducts well in solid and liquid, and it is malleable.

Good conduction in the solid means there must be delocalised electrons free to move. Malleability means layers of positive ions can slide over each other without shattering. That is the classic description of giant metallic bonding.

**State the change**

So the change is from a giant covalent lattice with localised electrons to a giant metallic lattice with delocalised electrons.

That is grey tin to white tin.

options.A: Incorrect. A giant ionic structure would conduct when molten because ions become mobile, but grey tin does not conduct even as a liquid. Also white tin conducts as a solid, which ionic solids never do.
options.B: Correct. Grey tin matches giant covalent: very high boiling point, non-conductor in solid and liquid, brittle due to rigid directional bonds. White tin matches giant metallic: very high boiling point, good conductor in solid and liquid due to delocalised electrons, malleable due to sliding layers of cations.
options.C: Incorrect. It gets the starting point wrong. Grey tin cannot be giant ionic because an ionic liquid would conduct, but grey tin shows no conductivity in solid or liquid.
options.D: Incorrect. Although white tin is correctly identified as metallic, grey tin is not ionic. Remember this is a pure element, tin only, so there are no oppositely charged different ions to make an ionic lattice, and the lack of conduction in the liquid rules ionic out.
